chunks: "For silicon, it comes straight from the periodic table. Silicon is Group IV with four valence electrons.
If I substitute a Group V atom, which has five, there's one extra electron, so it's a donor and gives N-type. The usual ones are phosphorus, arsenic and sometimes antimony.
If I substitute a Group III atom with three valence electrons, there's one fewer, so it's an acceptor and gives P-type.
The standard one is boron, and gallium, aluminium and indium are used in special cases. Which one you pick is about the process.
Arsenic is heavy and diffuses slowly, so it makes shallow, abrupt junctions, which is why it's used for source and drain.
Phosphorus diffuses faster and is used for deeper wells and for heavily doped layers. Boron is small, so it diffuses quickly and is the default P-type dopant.
For compound semiconductors it changes. In gallium arsenide, silicon sits on the gallium site and acts as a donor, and zinc or carbon give P-type.
In gallium nitride, silicon is the donor and magnesium is the acceptor."
